prior_response: Oh, I love the energy here because it feels very "direct-to-consumer" minimalist, almost like that pivot Patagonia made with their community-centric storytelling where they strip away the noise to focus on the core value proposition. The way you've laid out the order summary—specifically that bolding of the $39.99 for the mouse—it’s very "Amazon Prime" in its psychological anchoring, but then it jumps into this heavy payment block which reminds me of a fintech startup I consulted for last year where we struggled with the friction between 'add to cart' and 'checkout completion.' The hierarchy on that second button, the "Continue Shopping" being so prominent compared to the "Place Order," is such an interesting choice—it’s like what Nike does with their "Explore More" sections; it almost feels like you're giving them a safety net before they commit. I'm also seeing some really interesting visual weight in how the shipping is highlighted as 'FREE,' which is that classic 'loss aversion' play we see everywhere from SaaS platforms to heavy-hitting retail giants, and honestly, the way the information architecture flows from the item list straight into the card fields feels very much like a streamlined "one-click" philosophy even if it’s just a wireframe.

We want to understand what you meant by "The hierarchy on that second button, the "Continue Shopping" being so prominent compared to the "Place Order," is such an interesting choice", so let's go a bit deeper. Which of these best captures what you were pointing at?

A) The “Continue Shopping” button is positioned above “Place Order” and appears more visually prominent in the layout, making the shopping path feel higher priority than completing the order.

B) The “Place Order” button is lower on the screen and appears visually muted compared with the large “Continue Shopping” button, which makes the final checkout action feel buried.

C) The two buttons are grouped together beneath the payment details
turns.a: A and B are both basically the same problem from two camera angles, but if I had to pick the cleanest read, it’s A. The big black “Continue Shopping” button is sitting above the greyed-out “Place Order,” so my eye reads “leave checkout” before it reads “complete checkout,” which is wild in a secure checkout flow, like putting the exit sign brighter than the cash register. And yes, I get that “Place Order” may be disabled because the payment fields are empty, very Stripe/Shopify default logic, but visually the page is still teaching me that continuing shopping is the primary action. If the business goal is conversion, I’d expect “Place Order” to own that button territory once available, and “Continue Shopping” to feel secondary, smaller, or text-link-ish rather than the hero CTA.

turns.q: How does the placement and visual treatment of “Continue Shopping” above “Place Order” make it feel like the higher-priority action?
turns.a: Because the “Continue Shopping” button is full-width, black, high-contrast, and it appears first in the action stack, so it gets the combined advantage of position and contrast, which is basically the checkout equivalent of giving the supporting actor the movie poster. The “Place Order” button underneath is light grey with low-contrast text, so even though semantically it’s the transaction moment, visually it reads as unavailable, inactive, or almost afterthought-y, like a disabled SaaS upgrade button before you fill required fields. In marketing terms, the page is creating a CTA hierarchy where the escape route has the strongest brand voice and the revenue action is whispering, which is backwards unless the real goal is basket building rather than conversion. I’d keep the disabled state logic if fields are empty, sure, but I’d make “Continue Shopping” a secondary link or outline treatment, because right now the eye lands there before it ever processes the commitment action below.

turns.q: What design decision or gap causes the full-width black “Continue Shopping” button to receive stronger emphasis than the lighter “Place Order” button?
turns.a: The gap is that the design is treating “disabled” as “invisible,” so “Place Order” has lost almost all of its CTA authority while “Continue Shopping” is styled like the single primary brand action on the page. It’s not just color, although the black fill is doing a ton of work, like the old Apple Store checkout where the blue button owns the moment; it’s also that both buttons are the same full-width size, so the only differentiator left is visual weight, and black beats pale grey every time. The decision to put the secondary action above the transaction action compounds it, because users scan down from payment details and hit this big dark rectangle before they ever get to the actual purchase button. I’d either make “Continue Shopping” a text link near the top or under the order summary, and reserve the big filled button slot for “Place Order,” even if disabled, so the layout is still telling the right story before the form is complete.

turns.q: Which part of this wireframe makes the disabled “Place Order” state read as low-authority or invisible rather than still being the primary checkout action?
turns.a: It’s specifically the combination of the pale grey fill, pale grey “Place Order” label, and its placement directly underneath that huge black “Continue Shopping” bar, because the contrast gap is so extreme that the order button becomes more like legal copy than an action. And the funny thing is the page already has other low-emphasis elements, like the tiny “We accept Visa…” line and the terms text at the bottom, so visually “Place Order” is accidentally joining that family instead of staying in the CTA family, which is a classic brand hierarchy problem, not just a UX nit. If this were one of my retail clients, I’d say the disabled purchase button still needs to look like the destination, just temporarily locked, maybe darker outline, clearer disabled messaging, or the primary slot above the secondary action. Right now the wireframe is saying “shopping continues here” in a loud voice and “ordering maybe happens later” in a whisper.
